title: The Shared Enemy - Best Practices
author: Nicole Williams
summary: In this installment of her public learning journal, Nicole Williams synthesizes two influential but opposing thinkers on complex project management, Bent Flyvbjerg (How Big Things Get Done) and Dave Snowden (the Cynefin framework), around the shared starting point that 99.5 percent of megaprojects fail to meet budget, schedule, and benefits targets. She characterizes the two as intellectual allies who diagnose the same problem, traditional linear planning collapsing under unpredictable complexity, but prescribe opposite cures: Flyvbjerg wants to convert the unordered into the ordered using aggregated base rates and reference-class forecasting from similar past projects, while Snowden argues that forcing complex systems into order is precisely how they fail, advocating small, safe-to-fail probes and real-time sensing instead, since retrospective data cannot reliably predict emergent futures. Williams's practical synthesis is not to choose between them but to classify each project workstream first, using Flyvbjerg's outside-view forecasting for complicated, repeatable work (data migrations, infrastructure builds) and Snowden's probe-sense-respond approach for complex, emergent work (stakeholder alignment, governance adoption, behavior change), citing Healthcare.gov's recovery through small real-time probing teams as a case where treating a complex project as merely complicated caused the initial failure.
points: Williams's key diagnostic distinction, borrowed from Cynefin, is between 'complicated' work (sense first, then act, appropriate for Flyvbjerg's forecasting methods) and 'complex' work (probe first, then sense and respond, appropriate for Snowden's methods), arguing most project failures come from applying the wrong lens to the wrong type of work.

She grounds the stakes in Flyvbjerg's headline statistic that 99.5 percent of megaprojects fail to meet their budget, schedule, and benefits targets, framing the entire piece as a response to that failure rate rather than an abstract theoretical exercise.

Her synthesis explicitly rejects an either/or framing between historical-data forecasting and real-time experimentation, proposing instead a 'dual-delivery engine' that applies each method to different workstreams within the same project.

The Healthcare.gov case study operationalizes the framework concretely: she attributes its initial failure to treating an inherently complex, multi-stakeholder project as merely complicated, and its recovery to a small team empowered to probe, sense, and respond in real time.

Her practical uncertainty taxonomy (estimation uncertainty, technical uncertainty, emergent uncertainty), each mapped to a specific response method, gives project leaders a reusable triage tool for deciding which planning approach fits a given piece of work.
quotes: 99.5% of megaprojects fail to meet their budget, schedule, and benefits targets. (Flyvbjerg)
Snowden and Flyvbjerg are intellectual allies with opposing approaches to project management. They diagnose the same symptoms and prescribe different cures.
Snowden argues that forcing things into order is exactly how systems fail, and Flyvbjerg is trying to turn the unordered into the ordered.

Dave Snowden, on the other hand, warns against looking at a few successful companies, finding something they all do, and then saying, "Do this, and you will succeed." He says this mixes up things that happen together (correlation) with things that actually cause results (causation).

Know the type of project you have: Don't mistake a complex project for a complicated one. They operate differently and should be managed differently. Complicated is sense first. Complex is probe first.
For example, Healthcare.gov was actually a complex project but wasn't executed that way... They brought in a small team to probe, sense, and respond in real-time and it worked.
Pairing the outside view (Flyvbjerg) with the emergent view (Snowden) we can stop forcing a square peg into a round hole. Doing this we learn to slow down to speed up.
